Subject: RFP - network isolation and egress/attack-surface detail request

Karthik —

Thanks for the quick intro on Friday. As part of Arboreal's procurement RFP, our security team needs a concise packet covering: a network diagram of your hosted offering, the tenant isolation model (control plane vs data plane boundaries), egress control and allowlisting approach, and a 1-page threat model summary focused on lateral movement and data-exfiltration mitigations.

Can you provide:
- A single-sheet network topology diagram showing VPCs, sidecar/edge proxies, and outbound egress points
- A short summary of how tenant compute and KV caches are isolated (attack paths you consider highest risk)
- Any compensating controls (KMS/HSM, audit logs, SIEM integration, ephemeral creds)
- Links to SOC2 / network evidence if available (or a time estimate for delivery)

We'd like to review this before our technical deep-dive next week. If you have a short write-up and diagram that would be perfect. Please include any known limitations (e.g., shared control plane telemetry) so we can evaluate risk.

Thanks,
Tim

From: vanessa_ortiz@redwood.com
To: Tim Duncan <tim.duncan@arborealbank.com>
Cc: karthik_iyer@redwood.com, kimberly_park@redwood.com
Date: 2028-03-23T08:47:00-07:00
Subject: Redwood - Arboreal RFP: network isolation & threat model (summary + artifacts)

Tim / Arboreal team —

Attaching the packet requested. Quick executive summary first, then short appendix items.

Executive summary (TL;DR)
- Deployment modes: Hosted (multitenant), Dedicated (single-tenant GPU pool), Private (VPC/VPN or on-prem). For RFP we're focusing on Hosted + Dedicated options.
- Isolation model: data plane is logically isolated per-customer using per-tenant network namespaces and VM/GPU slice isolation. Control plane (orchestration, model catalog) is shared but segmented with strict RBAC, mTLS for control channels, and encrypted persisted state.
- Egress controls: outbound traffic originates from dedicated egress proxies per-deployment, allowlist via egress VPC endpoints (customer-managed allowlisting possible for Dedicated/private), and optional per-tenant NAT gateway with route tables.
- High-risk attack paths identified: compromised model sidecar leading to KV-cache access, lateral movement between co-located workloads if hypervisor escape or container breakout, and malicious exfil over allowed egress destination(s).

Key mitigations (short)
- Network: per-tenant subnets + NSGs, micro-segmentation at process boundary using sidecar proxies (TLS-enforced), and forced egress via dedicated proxy/NAT.
- Auth & secrets: KMS-backed keys (customer KMS support via BYOK for Dedicated/Private), HSM for signing critical artifacts, short-lived tokens for model infra with automatic rotation.
- Runtime defenses: continuous KV-cache ACLs, strict kernel hardening, seccomp profiles, and limited inline model eval permissions.
- Observability & detection: token-level tracing, per-request audit logs to immutable store, integration hooks for SIEM/SOC via structured logs and optional Syslog/HTTP forwarding.

Attachment list (included):
- redwood_network_topology_v2.png — single-sheet diagram (VPCs, proxies, data/control plane flows)
- redwood_egress_controls_summary.pdf — narrative + table of egress controls and configuration options
- evidence_s3_access_logs.zip — sample redacted flow logs and S3 access events (anonymized)

Short appendix: components and flows (abbreviated)
1) Ingress & request handling
   - Customer request hits edge proxy (public LB). Edge performs TLS termination and forwards to tenant-specific sidecar over mTLS.
   - Sidecar enforces request-level RBAC and enqueues work to serving runtime.

2) Serving runtime & KV cache isolation
   - Each tenant gets an isolated serving partition (namespace + process group). KV cache namespaces are keyed-per-tenant; access tokens are scoped and short-lived.
   - KVs persist to a customer-isolated store where possible (Dedicated) or logically partitioned store (Hosted).

3) Control plane vs data plane
   - Control plane services (model catalog, rollout manager) run in a separate VPC with no direct data-plane access. Control plane calls are authenticated and logged; runtime exposes a narrow control API over mTLS.

4) Egress & outbound allowlisting
   - All outbound flows must traverse egress proxies which enforce destination allowlists. By default outbound is restricted to: customer-specified storage endpoints, model artifact mirror endpoints, and telemetry sinks.
   - For Dedicated/private we support customer-managed VPC peering and direct connect so customers can enforce traffic inspection on their side.

5) Threat model highlights and residual risk
   - Lateral movement: mitigated via strong process isolation, kernel hardening, and network micro-segmentation. Residual risk: hypervisor/container escape — addressed by patch cadence and third-party vulnerability scanning.
   - Data exfil: mitigated by allowlist egress proxies, anomaly detection on request patterns, and auditing. Residual risk: credential compromise leading to allowed-destination exfil — mitigated by short-lived creds and KMS attestation.

Follow-ups / asks for Arboreal to help us scope:
- Do you require all egress destinations to be customer-managed? (This affects our recommended Dedicated setup.)
- Any regulatory constraints on telemetry retention or SIEM integration (e.g., only on-prem SIEM ingestion)?

Call to action
- We uploaded the packet to your Drive link and attached the three artifacts to this thread. If you want a short walkthrough we can do 30 minutes Mon 3/26 or Tue 3/27 (your timezone).

Vanessa Ortiz
Security Architect, Redwood Inference
vanessa_ortiz@redwood.com

Attachments: redwood_network_topology_v2.png (diagram), redwood_egress_controls_summary.pdf, evidence_s3_access_logs.zip
